title: Drinking Up to Five Cups of Coffee a Day May Lower Stroke and Diabetes Risk, Major Study Finds
excerpt: An umbrella review of over 100 meta-analyses finds consistent evidence that moderate coffee consumption is associated with reduced risk of several chronic diseases, though experts caution results vary by preparation method.
body:
• An umbrella review of more than 100 meta-analyses found that drinking three to five cups of coffee daily is associated with a lower risk of stroke, type 2 diabetes and several other chronic conditions.
  • The review found the strongest protective associations for type 2 diabetes, with moderate consumption linked to up to a 30% risk reduction.
  • Benefits appear to vary by preparation method, with filtered coffee showing the most consistent positive associations.
  • Researchers caution that the findings are observational and do not prove causation; individual tolerance, pregnancy and certain conditions require separate consideration.

Moderate coffee consumption — in the range of three to five cups per day — is associated with a reduced risk of stroke, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and several other chronic conditions, according to a comprehensive umbrella review that synthesised findings from more than 100 published meta-analyses.

The review, which examined the accumulated evidence on coffee's effects on human health, found consistent protective associations across multiple disease categories. The findings add to a growing body of research that has shifted the medical consensus on coffee from cautious scepticism to qualified endorsement over the past two decades.

Strongest Evidence for Diabetes Protection

"For the roughly two billion cups consumed globally each day, the review suggests that for most adults, their morning habit is doing more good than harm."

The most robust associations emerged for type 2 diabetes, where moderate coffee consumption was linked to risk reductions of up to 30 percent compared to non-drinkers. The effect appeared to follow a dose-response pattern, with benefits plateauing at around four to five cups daily.

For stroke, the review found that moderate consumption was associated with a lower risk of both ischaemic and haemorrhagic events, although the magnitude of the effect was smaller than for diabetes. Similar protective patterns were observed for Parkinson's disease, certain liver conditions including cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, and depression.

Preparation Method Matters

Not all coffee is created equal when it comes to health outcomes. The review noted that filtered coffee — which removes oily compounds called diterpenes — showed the most consistent positive associations. Unfiltered preparations, such as French press or boiled coffee, retain higher levels of cafestol and kahweol, which can raise LDL cholesterol levels.

The distinction is particularly relevant for South Asian coffee traditions. South Indian filter coffee, prepared using a metal drip device, effectively filters out many of these compounds, potentially placing it among the healthier preparation methods. Instant coffee, by contrast, showed weaker and sometimes opposite associations in some studies, a finding that echoes recent research linking filtered coffee to slower biological aging.

Important Caveats

Researchers emphasised that the findings are observational — drawn from population studies that track coffee consumption alongside health outcomes — and do not establish that coffee directly prevents disease. Confounding factors, including diet, exercise, socioeconomic status and genetic variation in caffeine metabolism, could influence the results.

The review also noted that the protective associations do not apply uniformly. Pregnant women are advised to limit caffeine intake due to established risks, and individuals with certain heart arrhythmias, anxiety disorders or acid reflux conditions may need to moderate consumption. The beneficial range of three to five cups assumes standard 8-ounce servings of brewed coffee, not the concentrated espresso shots or oversized specialty drinks that are increasingly common.

Despite these caveats, the consistency of the evidence across more than 100 separate meta-analyses is striking. For the roughly two billion cups consumed globally each day, the review suggests that for most adults, their morning habit is doing more good than harm.
